1. Survivorship Bias in Plain English

The crucial point is that the bias does not need anyone to cheat. Nobody deletes the losers on purpose. Closed funds stop reporting, delisted tickers vanish from the vendor file the analyst happens to download, and defaulted borrowers are archived to a different system. What makes survivorship bias distinctive is its direction. Most sampling problems add noise or a bias of unknown sign. Removing the failures almost always pushes estimated returns up and estimated risk down, so it produces exactly the kind of result people are hoping to find.

Two lessons fall straight out of the formula. First, the bias is proportional to σ. Double the dispersion of the population and you double the fake alpha, which is why survivorship matters far more for hedge funds, small caps and emerging market equities than for investment-grade bond funds. Second, the bias grows with the attrition rate

Notice what the formula does not contain: the true mean. The bias is added on top of whatever the true average is. A population with genuinely negative average alpha after fees can therefore look flat or positive once the failures leave the room, which is a far more damaging outcome than an exaggerated but still positive number.

Removing the worst paths also removes the worst drawdowns, so volatility, tail risk and maximum drawdown estimates are flattered too. A risk model calibrated on survivors understates the loss distribution it is supposed to describe.

Probability of default models must be estimated on cohorts that retain defaults, withdrawals and early repayments. Data migrations are a prime moment for defaulted names to vanish, so the default count should be reconciled before and after any system change.
